questions.question: Describe the events from the moment a pollen grain lands on a stigma until fertilisation takes place.
questions.expected_answer: The pollen grain germinates on the stigma, stimulated by sugary liquid, and grows a pollen tube. The tube grows down through the stigma and style towards the ovary, carrying the male gametes near its tip, guided by chemical signals from the ovule. It enters an ovule through the micropyle and bursts, releasing the male gametes. One male gamete fuses with the egg cell to form a zygote; this fusion is fertilisation.

questions.question: State what each of the following becomes after fertilisation: ovule, ovary, zygote, petals. Explain why a tomato is a fruit in science.
questions.expected_answer: Ovule becomes the seed; ovary becomes the fruit; zygote becomes the embryo (radicle, plumule and cotyledons); petals (with stamens, stigma and style) wither and fall off. A tomato develops from the ovary of the flower and contains seeds, so it is a fruit in the scientific sense, even though it is eaten as a vegetable.

questions.question: Explain why seed dispersal is important and describe four methods of dispersal, each with an adaptation and an example.
questions.expected_answer: Dispersal reduces competition between seedlings and with the parent for light, water and minerals, and allows plants to colonise new areas. Animals: fleshy fruits eaten and seeds passed in droppings (marula eaten by elephants), or hooks that catch on fur (blackjacks), or elaiosomes carried by ants (fynbos). Wind: wings or hairy parachutes (pine seeds, dandelions). Water: light, air-filled, waterproof fruits that float (coconut). Self-dispersal: pods that dry, twist and burst open to fling seeds (beans, peas).
